title: Evaluating the quality of online health information: A comparative study of COPD patient information in Facebook forums versus ChatGPT
screen_reason: Content analysis of 2,748 comments on 48 posts each from a Danish and an international English-language COPD Facebook group (October 2024 content). Three medically trained reviewers coded every relevant comment as 'useful' (scientifically accurate), 'misleading' (containing at least one scientifically unproven detail) or 'neither', with Fleiss' kappa reported. This yields shares of items coded misleading, with explicit denominators, for each language group overall and for the subset of comments giving actionable advice — CONTENT prevalences.

estimates.country: Denmark (Danish-language COPD Facebook group, approx. 4,700 members)
estimates.platform: Facebook (open-access COPD patient group, post comments)
estimates.date: All posts and comments from October 2024 (extracted 16 Jan - 1 Feb 2025)
estimates.measure_type: % of relevant comments in the Danish COPD Facebook group coded as misleading by clinician reviewers
estimates.denominator: 667 comments judged relevant (i.e. directly responding to the posted question) out of the 1,433 comments on the 48 October-2024 posts in the Danish group
estimates.definition: Comment classified 'misleading' because it contained at least one scientifically unproven detail; comments containing scientifically accurate information were 'useful' and those making no factual claim (e.g. purely personal experience) were 'neither'
estimates.misinfo_def: "A comment was classified as 'useful' if it contained scientifically accurate information, while comments containing at least one scientifically unproven detail were labeled as 'misleading'."
estimates.source_quote: In the Danish group, 34% (n = 231) were 'useful', 9% (n = 62) were 'misleading', and 57% (n = 384) were 'neither'.
estimates.page_loc: Results 3.1.2 (also Abstract: "In the Danish group, 47% (667/1,433) of comments were relevant, with 34% deemed useful and 9% misleading")
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three medically trained authors with clinical COPD/respiratory experience coded independently after a 20-statement calibration exercise (pilot items excluded from analysis), then met to resolve discrepancies to full consensus. Fleiss' kappa 0.89 (95% CI 0.87-0.91) for relevance screening and 0.76 (0.73-0.80) for the useful/misleading/neither classification; ICC 0.79 for the Likert ratings.
estimates.moderator_quote: During this period, all posts and comments from October 2024 in the Danish group were systematically collected, resulting in 48 posts and 1,433 comments. ... For Facebook, all comments were first assessed for relevance to the original post. ... Comments deemed irrelevant were excluded from further evaluation.
estimates.notes: Denominator is RELEVANT comments (667), not all 1,433 extracted comments — 53% of the Danish thread content was irrelevant and excluded before coding, which raises the share substantially relative to an all-comments denominator. borderline = true because 'misleading' is defined as containing at least one scientifically UNPROVEN detail, which is broader than false and could in principle catch a claim that is true but unevidenced; the coding is nevertheless an explicit misleading label applied by clinicians against scientific evidence, so CONTENT rather than QUALITY. value_pct given as the exact part/whole 62/667 = 9.3% (the paper's '9%' is a rounding). denom_selection = single_source: one Facebook group; sampling_frame = full_census within that group for that month.

estimates.platform: Facebook (open-access COPD patient group, post comments)

estimates.denominator: 734 comments judged relevant out of the 1,315 comments on the 48 most-engaged October-2024 posts in the English-language group
estimates.definition: Comment classified 'misleading' because it contained at least one scientifically unproven detail
estimates.misinfo_def: "A comment was classified as 'useful' if it contained scientifically accurate information, while comments containing at least one scientifically unproven detail were labeled as 'misleading'."
estimates.source_quote: Similarly, in the English group, 38% (n = 278) were 'useful', 9% (n = 63) were 'misleading', and 53% (n = 393) were 'neither'.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same three clinician reviewers, same codebook and calibration; Fleiss' kappa 0.89 for relevance and 0.76 for the useful/misleading/neither classification.

estimates.platform: Facebook (open-access COPD patient group, post comments)
estimates.date: All posts and comments from October 2024
estimates.measure_type: % of Danish-group comments giving actionable medical advice (behavioural change) that were coded misleading
estimates.value_raw: 34 of 211 comments encouraging behavioral change were misleading (16.1%, 95% CI 11.4%-21.8%)
estimates.denominator: 211 comments in the Danish group coded as encouraging behavioural change, i.e. providing specific actionable medical advice (e.g. medication adjustment, inhalation technique)
estimates.definition: Comment giving actionable medical advice that was also classified 'misleading' (contained at least one scientifically unproven detail)
estimates.misinfo_def: "Behavioral change encompassed comments encouraging health-related modifications (any statement providing specific actionable medical advice (e.g. medication adjustment or inhalation techniques)"
estimates.source_quote: In the Danish group, 211 comments encouraged behavioral change, of which 34 (16.1%, 95% CI: 11.4% - 21.8%) were classified as misleading.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three clinician reviewers; Fleiss' kappa 0.81 (95% CI 0.77-0.84) for identifying behavioural-change advice, 0.76 for the misleading classification.
estimates.moderator_quote: A sub-analysis focused on comments encouraging behavioral change, defined as actionable medical advice.
estimates.notes: Narrower denominator than the 9.3% row (advice-giving comments only), hence definition_variant = true; the paper flags this as its headline risk finding ('Concerns were greatest for advice-oriented content'). Note 211 is not a subset of the 667 relevant comments in any way the paper states — behavioural-change coding was applied as a separate category, so the two rows should not be treated as nested without checking.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) NO ChatGPT row, and this is the main judgement call. The paper applied the identical useful/misleading/neither scheme to 96 ChatGPT-4o responses but never reports how many were classified misleading, and its two statements about ChatGPT inaccuracy contradict each other: the Discussion says ChatGPT's answers were 'consistently high quality, with only a single inaccurate recommendation identified', while Results 3.2 says 'Table 2S shows the taxonomy and frequency of inaccuracies in ChatGPT-responses (n = 14)'. Whether n = 14 counts inaccurate responses or individual inaccuracies (possibly several per response) cannot be settled from the text, and Table 2S is supplementary and not in this file. Neither 1/96 nor 14/96 is stated, so under R8 no ChatGPT value is extractable. An adjudicator with the supplement should revisit this: a chatbot CONTENT row (denom_scope topical, sampling_frame curated_seed, platform other/LLM) would otherwise be extractable. 2) Likert quality ratings (Facebook median 4.0, ChatGPT 5.0, with Hodges-Lehmann differences) are scale medians, not shares, so no row per the governing rule; they are also a quality/accuracy severity scale applied only to comments already coded useful or misleading. 3) Not extracted: the relevance shares (47% Danish, 56% English) — relevance is not veracity; the 'useful' shares (34%, 38%) and 'neither' shares (57%, 53%) — complements, not misinformation. 4) A minor inconsistency: the Abstract says '2,761 comments' while the Results give 1,433 + 1,315 = 2,748; and the Abstract reports the English relevance share only as a count (734/1,315) whereas Results give 56%. Neither affects the extracted denominators. 5) Table 1 and Table 2 disagree on some topic counts (e.g. Medication 9 (19%) in Table 1 vs 9 (17%) in Table 2; Exercise 6 (13%) vs 7 (15%)); topic distributions were not extracted. 6) Figures from a prior Danish atopic-disease study (12% misleading vs 11% useful; 52% of behaviour-change comments inaccurate) are cited from elsewhere and excluded under R8. 7) No RECALL/EXPOSURE/SHARING measures: reactions per post are engagement counts with no misinformation share attached.

rob.design: Cross-sectional comparative content analysis. Two open-access COPD Facebook groups found by searching Facebook Groups in Danish ('KOL', 'Kronisk Obstruktiv Lungesygdom') and English ('COPD', 'Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease'); Danish group approx. 4,700 members, international English group approx. 12,500. Danish sample = a full census of all 48 posts and 1,433 comments from October 2024; English sample = the 48 most-engaged October-2024 posts and their 1,315 comments, chosen to match the Danish n. Extraction 16 Jan - 1 Feb 2025; October chosen to give a ~3-month settling interval. Each post also submitted verbatim to ChatGPT-4o on 3 Feb 2025 in a fresh incognito account with default settings and no browsing (96 prompts). Coding: relevance screen, then useful / misleading / neither, then a 5-point Likert accuracy rating for useful and misleading items; three medically trained COPD-experienced authors coded independently after a 20-item calibration pilot (excluded from analysis), with consensus discussion afterwards. Reliability: Fleiss' kappa 0.89 (relevance), 0.76 (useful/misleading/neither), 0.81 (behavioural-change identification); ICC 0.79 (Likert). Pre-specified primary endpoint for part 1 was the proportion of comments classified misleading. Analysis in R 4.3.1; Wilcoxon signed-rank / rank-sum. No ethics approval required (anonymised public data). Authors' stated limits: single month of data, some subjectivity in clinician rating, only one LLM assessed, LLM outputs change over time.
rob.item6_quote: A comment was classified as 'useful' if it contained scientifically accurate information, while comments containing at least one scientifically unproven detail were labeled as 'misleading'. Comments that did not fall into either of these categories were marked as 'neither' and were not subjected to further analysis.
rob.item10_quote: In the Danish group, 34% (n = 231) were 'useful', 9% (n = 62) were 'misleading', and 57% (n = 384) were 'neither'. Similarly, in the English group, 38% (n = 278) were 'useful', 9% (n = 63) were 'misleading', and 53% (n = 393) were 'neither'.
